profile.name: The Maid of Cashmere
profile.tagline: A 19th-century opéra-ballet featuring divine tests and a signature shawl dance.
profile.insight: In the 1833 Drury Lane production, the god Brama tests his lover Zelica’s devotion by feigning interest in two other bayadères before revealing his divinity to save her from an impending execution.
profile.profile: The Maid of Cashmere is a 19th-century English opéra-ballet that premiered at Drury Lane on March 16, 1833. It served as an adaptation of the French work Le Dieu et la Bayadère by Eugène Scribe and Daniel Auber, featuring music by Auber and revisions by Henry Bishop and Edward Fitzball. The production is historically significant for introducing the French dancer Pauline Duvernay to London audiences and for its inclusion of a distinctive shawl dance. The narrative follows the god Brama as he assumes human form to test the loyalty of the bayadère Zelica.
profile.profile_long:
The Maid of Cashmere stands as a representative example of the 1830s London stage, where the boundaries between opera and ballet were frequently blurred to satisfy the tastes of the Romantic era. Premiering on March 16, 1833, at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, the work was an English-language adaptation of the French opéra-ballet 'Le Dieu et la Bayadère,' originally created by the librettist Eugène Scribe and the composer Daniel Auber. The London production involved a collaborative effort to localize the work, with the English composer Henry Bishop and the dramatist Edward Fitzball contributing to the adaptation of Auber’s original score and narrative structure.

The production was a vehicle for the promotion of international talent, most notably the French ballerina Pauline Duvernay, who performed the leading role of Zelica. The casting of Duvernay, alongside the inclusion of a foreign corps de ballet, was a strategic choice by the Drury Lane management to bring the prestige of the Parisian stage to an English audience. The role of Zelica was also performed by Madame Céleste, indicating the importance of the lead dancer's technical and dramatic capability in carrying the production's narrative arc.

At the heart of the performance was a narrative of divine intervention and romantic trial. The plot centers on Brama, a deity who descends to earth in human form to experience mortal suffering and, more importantly, to identify a woman capable of true, selfless love. As a fugitive hiding in the city of Cashmere, Brama encounters Zelica, a bayadère who remains steadfast in her affection for him despite the pressures of the Grand Vizier. The dramatic tension of the piece relies on a series of tests orchestrated by Brama, who feigns interest in two other bayadères—Leila, a singer, and Fatima, a dancer—to provoke Zelica’s jealousy and confirm her loyalty. The climax of the performance occurs when Brama reveals his true divine nature to rescue Zelica from a death sentence, ultimately ascending with her to the heavens.

Beyond the narrative, the production is remembered for its specific choreographic elements, most notably the 'shawl dance.' While the specific steps of this dance are not detailed in the sources, its inclusion was a hallmark of the production's visual appeal, utilizing the shawl as a prop to enhance the movement of the female dancers. The work remains a historical artifact of the 19th-century fascination with 'orientalist' themes, which were common in the balletic repertoire of the time. As an opéra-ballet, the work required a synthesis of vocal performance and dance, demanding that the performers move fluidly between the demands of the opera house and the ballet stage. The production's legacy is tied to its role in the cross-channel exchange of theatrical practices during the 1830s, documenting a moment when London audiences were increasingly exposed to the technical rigor and narrative conventions of the French Romantic ballet tradition.

claims.text: The Maid of Cashmere made its debut in March 1833 at Drury Lane.
claims.quote: The Maid of Cashmere made its debut in March 1833, combining elements of opera and ballet. It was performed for the first time at Drury Lane on March 16, 1833.

claims.text: The production was an English version of the French opéra-ballet Le Dieu et la Bayadère.
claims.quote: It was the English version of La bayadère amoureuse, ou, Le dieu et la bayadère, Eugène Scribe and Daniel Auber's popular piece.

claims.text: The production featured a shawl dance performed by the female dancers.
claims.quote: The production aimed to introduce Mlle. Duvernay and the foreign corps de ballet, featuring a shawl dance performed by the female dancers.

claims.text: Pauline Duvernay and Madame Céleste played the lead role of Zelica.
claims.quote: In its debut in March 1833, the French ballet dancer Pauline Duvernay was featured in the leading role of Zelica. The lead role of Zelica was also played by Madame Céleste.

claims.text: The narrative involves the god Brama testing Zelica's love by feigning interest in other bayadères.
claims.quote: To test Zelica's love and loyalty, Brama stirs her jealousy by showing interest first in Leila, a singing Bayadère, and then in Fatima, a dancing Bayadère.
